'''''Dysphania ambrosioides''''', formerly ''Chenopodium ambrosioides'', known as '''epazote''', '''Jesuit's tea''', '''Mexican tea'''<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17}}</ref> or '''wormseed''',<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN |access-date=2024-06-23}}</ref> is an annual or short-lived perennial [[herb]] native to the Americas.

==Description==
''Dysphania ambrosioides'' is an [[annual plant|annual]] or short-lived [[perennial]] herb, growing to {{convert|1.2|m|ft|abbr=on|frac=2}} tall, irregularly branched, with oblong-[[lanceolate]] [[leaf|leaves]] up to {{convert|12|cm|in|frac=2|abbr=on}} long. The [[flower]]s are small and green, produced in a branched [[panicle]] at the apex of the stem.

As well as in its native areas, it is grown in warm [[temperate]] to [[subtropical]] areas of Europe and the United States ([[Missouri]], [[New England]], [[Eastern US]]),<ref name=Grieve>{{cite book | title = A Modern Herbal | author = Mrs. M. Grieve | date = June 1971 | publisher = FRHS | page = 854 | isbn = 0-486-22798-7}}</ref> sometimes becoming an [[invasive species|invasive]] [[weed]].

=== Chemistry ===
[[File:Dysphania ambrosioides MHNT.BOT.2012.10.16.jpg|thumb|upright=1.3|''Dysphania ambrosioides'' – [[MHNT]]]]

Epazote [[essential oil]] contains [[ascaridole]] (up to 70%), [[limonene]], [[p-cymene]], and smaller amounts of numerous other [[terpene|monoterpenes]] and monoterpene derivatives ({{nowrap|[[pinene|α-pinene]]}}, [[myrcene]], [[terpinene]], [[thymol]], [[camphor]] and trans-isocarveol). [[Ascaridole]] (1,4-peroxido-p-menth-2-ene) is rather an uncommon constituent of spices; another plant owing much of its character to this monoterpene [[peroxide]] is [[boldo]]. Ascaridole is slightly toxic and has a pungent, not very pleasant flavor. In pure form, [[ascaridole]] decomposes violently upon heating, but this is relatively weak in regards to energy release, since breaking the oxygen bond will not destroy the entire molecule.<ref>{{cite web |date=29 October 2020 |title=Epazote: Organic Peroxides from a Plant |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JwTCG15ZB4s |url-status=live |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211212/JwTCG15ZB4s |archive-date=2021-12-12 |website=[[YouTube]] |quote=YouTube video name: 'Epazote: Organic Peroxides from a Plant'}}{{cbignore}}</ref> Ascaridole content is lower in epazote from Mexico than in epazote grown in Europe or Asia.<ref>{{cite magazine |last=Laferrière |first=Joseph E. |date=21 June 1990 |title=Nutritional and pharmacological properties of yerbaníz, epazote, and Mountain Pima oregano |url=https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/0157/0808/files/SeedheadNews29-1990.pdf |magazine=Seedhead News |publisher=Native Seeds/SEARCH |page=9 |number=29}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
The species was described in 1753 by [[Carl Linnaeus]] as ''Chenopodium ambrosioides''.<ref>{{LSP1|219}}</ref> Some researchers treated it as a highly polymorphic species with several subspecies. Today these are considered as their own species within genus [[Dysphania (plant)|''Dysphania'']] (e.g. American wormseed, ''Chenopodium ambrosioides'' var. ''anthelminticum'' is now accepted as ''[[Dysphania anthelmintica]]'').<ref>Steven E. Clemants & Sergei L. Mosyakin (2003): [http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=304226 ''Dysphania sect. Adenois'' - online] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190916082408/http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=304226 |date=2019-09-16 }}. In: Flora of North America Editorial Committee (ed.): ''Flora of North America North of Mexico. Volume 4: Magnoliophyta: Caryophyllidae, part 1''. Oxford University Press, New York, {{ISBN|0-19-517389-9}}, p. 269.</ref><ref>Steven E. Clemants & Sergei L. Mosyakin (2003): [http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=242415382 ''Dysphania anthelmintica'' - online] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304132302/http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=242415382 |date=2016-03-04 }}. In: Flora of North America Editorial Committee (ed.): ''Flora of North America North of Mexico. Volume 4: Magnoliophyta: Caryophyllidae, part 1''. Oxford University Press, New York, {{ISBN|0-19-517389-9}}, p. 269.</ref>

The generic name ''Dysphania'' was traditionally applied in the 1930s to some species endemic to Australia. Placement and rank of this taxon have ranged from a mere section within ''Chenopodium'' to the sole genus of a separate family, Dysphaniaceae, or a representative of the Illicebraceae. The close affinity of ''Dysphania'' to "glandular" species of ''Chenopodium'' ''sensu lato'' is now evident.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=111141|title=Dysphania in Flora of North America @ efloras.org|work=efloras.org|access-date=2013-06-29|archive-date=2013-10-12|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131012183621/http://efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=111141|url-status=live}}</ref>

The specific epithet ''ambrosioides'' refers to the plant's resemblance to unrelated plants of the genus ''[[Ambrosia (genus)|Ambrosia]]'', in the aster family.

==Etymology==
The common Spanish name {{lang|es|epazote}} (sometimes spelled and pronounced {{lang|es|ipasote}} or {{lang|es|ypasote}}) is derived from the [[Nahuatl language|Nahuatl]] word {{lang|nah|epazōtl}} ({{IPA|nah|eˈpasoːt͡ɬ|pron}}).

== Toxicity ==
Humans have died from overdoses of ''D. ambrosioides'' essential oils (attributed to the [[ascaridole]] content). Symptoms include severe [[gastroenteritis]] with pain, [[vomiting]], and [[diarrhea]],<ref>{{cite book |author=Tampion, John |title=Dangerous Plants |date=1977 |publisher=David and Charles |isbn=0715373757 |page=64 |chapter=''Chenopodium ambrosioides'' L.}}</ref> [[dizziness]], headache, temporary deafness, kidney and liver damage, convulsions, paralysis, death.<ref name="FH">{{Cite journal |last=Abid Aqsa, Mushtaq Ahmad, Muhammad Zafar, Sadia Zafar, Mohamed Fawzy Ramadan, Ashwaq T. Althobaiti, Shazia Sultana, Omer Kilic, Trobjon Makhkamov, Akramjon Yuldashev, Oybek Mamarakhimov, Khislat Khaydarov, Afat O. Mammadova, Komiljon Komilov |first=and Salman Majeed |date=December 2023 |title=Foliar epidermal and trichome micromorphological diversity among poisonous plants and their taxonomic significance |journal=[[Folia Horticulturae]] |language=en |volume=35 |issue=2 |pages=243–274 |doi=10.2478/fhort-2023-0019 |issn=2083-5965 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Uses ==

===Culinary===
[[File:Dysphania ambrosioides 717594901.jpg|thumb|''Dysphania ambrosioides'' leaves]]

Ideally collected before going to seed, ''D. ambrosioides'' is used as a [[leaf vegetable]], [[herb]], and [[herbal tea]],<ref name=Nyerges/> for its strong aroma and flavor. The fragrance of ''D. ambrosioides'' is strong and unique.<ref name=Nyerges/> Raw, it has a resinous, medicinal aroma, similar to [[oregano]], [[anise]], [[fennel]], or even [[tarragon]], but stronger. A common analogy is to [[turpentine]] or [[creosote]]. It has also been compared to [[citrus]], [[Satureja|savory]], and [[Mentha|mint]].

Although it is traditionally used with [[black turtle bean|black beans]] for flavor and its [[antiflatulent]] properties,<ref name=Nyerges>{{cite book |last1=Nyerges |first1=Christopher |title=Foraging Wild Edible Plants of North America: More than 150 Delicious Recipes Using Nature's Edibles |date=2016 |publisher=Rowman & Littlefield |isbn=978-1-4930-1499-6 |pages=73–75 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RwDHCgAAQBAJ}}</ref> it is also sometimes used to flavor other traditional Mexican dishes: it can be used to season [[quesadilla]]s and [[sope (food)|sopes]] (especially those containing [[huitlacoche]]), soups, [[mole de olla]], [[tamale]]s with [[cheese]] and [[chili pepper]]s, [[chilaquiles]], eggs and potatoes, [[esquites]], and [[enchilada]]s. It is often cooked into fried white rice, and it is an important ingredient for making the green salsa for chilaquiles.

In the [[Philippines]], where it is called ''pasotes'' or ''pasyotes'', it is a characteristic herb of [[Vigan]] ''pipian'', a chicken porridge distinct from the namesake [[Pipián (sauce)|Mexican pipian]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Love letter to Vigan (And Vegans) |website=[[The Philippine STAR]] |url=https://www.philstar.com/lifestyle/food-and-leisure/2018/05/03/1811499/love-letter-vigan-and-vegans |access-date=2025-03-24 |archive-date=2025-04-30 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250430080755/https://www.philstar.com/lifestyle/food-and-leisure/2018/05/03/1811499/love-letter-vigan-and-vegans |url-status=live }}</ref> It is also used in the [[Longaniza|longganisa]] of [[Sampaloc, Quezon|Sampaloc]], [[Quezon]], and as a stuffing for [[suckling pig|lechon]] in [[Carcar]], [[Cebu]].

===Agricultural===
The essential oils of ''D. ambrosioides'' contain [[terpene]] compounds, some of which have natural pesticide capabilities.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Isman |first=Murray B. |date=2020-04-01 |title=Commercial development of plant essential oils and their constituents as active ingredients in bioinsecticides |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s11101-019-09653-9 |journal=Phytochemistry Reviews |language=en |volume=19 |issue=2 |pages=235–241 |doi=10.1007/s11101-019-09653-9 |bibcode=2020PChRv..19..235I |s2cid=209596487 |issn=1572-980X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The compound [[ascaridole]] in epazote inhibits the growth of nearby species, so it is best to grow it at a distance from other plants.<ref>J. Jimenez-Osorio, Am. J. Bot. 78:139, 1991{{full citation needed|date=June 2019}}, cited in {{cite web |date=June 2012 |url=http://aggie-horticulture.tamu.edu/newsletters/hortupdate/2012/jun/epazote.html |title=Epazote (Chenopodium ambrosioides) |access-date=2013-02-13 |first=Cynthia W. |last=Mueller |website=Aggie Horticulture |publisher=Texas A & M University |archive-date=2015-09-30 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150930040734/http://aggie-horticulture.tamu.edu/newsletters/hortupdate/2012/jun/epazote.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

===Companion plant===
''Dysphania ambrosioides'' not only contains terpene compounds, but it also delivers partial protection to nearby plants simply by masking their scent to some insects, making it a useful [[companion plant]]. Its small flowers may also attract some predatory wasps and flies.
